strengths: Timely and important contribution: First comprehensive safety analysis of dLLMs with novel vulnerability decomposition (intra-step vs inter-step), particularly the Denoising-path Dependence finding which provides genuine new insights into dLLM generation mechanics

Well-motivated and elegant defense design: Stochastic Annealing Remasking with step-aware decay (Eq. 8) elegantly addresses safety-quality tradeoff by concentrating randomness early; Block-level Audit and Repair grounded in representation-based safety research

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 4 dLLM models, multiple attack paradigms (6 methods), diverse datasets, general capability preservation (MMLU, GSM8K, HumanEval), latency analysis, ablations, and hyperparameter sensitivity studies

Strong empirical results: 33.2% relative ASR reduction (47.9%→14.7%) across diverse attacks with negligible performance degradation and inference overhead; consistent improvements across different models
Practical and deployable: Training-free framework functions as plug-and-play module, improving real-world adoption prospects
Strong reproducibility: Detailed hyperparameters (Tables 3-6), algorithm specification (Appendix D), comprehensive experimental setup documentation, and code availability promised
weaknesses: Limited dLLM-specific attack evaluation: Only 2 true dLLM-specific attacks tested (PAD, DIJA); most attacks adapted from AR LLM literature (GCG, AutoDAN). Unclear if evaluated attacks represent optimal dLLM-specific threats. Critical for a safety paper at top venue.

Safety Divergence metric lacks rigorous validation: Eq. 9 uses heuristic cosine distance of mean hidden states at output layer, step 1 without sufficient justification. Missing: ablation on metric choice/layer/step; validation against alternatives; analysis of adaptive attacks circumventing detection via knowledge of threshold

Hyperparameter sensitivity undermines portability: α₀ varies 0.3-0.7 across models (Table 6); no principled selection strategy for new models. Contradicts 'plug-and-play' claim. Sensitivity analysis (Table 7-8) shows non-trivial performance gaps (≤8% ASR variation)

Block-level Repair applied only to first block: Defense ignores harmful content emerging in later blocks. Justification based on efficiency insufficient for safety-critical application. Missing analysis of attack fraction exploiting later blocks

No evaluation against adaptive attacks: Threat model assumes attackers unaware of DIFFUGUARD. No white-box adversarial evaluation where attackers know defense mechanisms and hyperparameters. Safety of heuristic metrics unvalidated

Weak baseline comparisons: Only 2 baselines (PPL-Filter, Self-reminder). Self-reminder produces dramatic improvements (93.65%→30.58% on LLaDA PAD), suggesting orthogonal defenses confound DIFFUGUARD contribution. Missing comparisons to guided decoding, representation-based methods

Insufficient statistical rigor: No error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests reported. Some 0.00% baseline ASR values (e.g., GCG on Dream) appear suspiciously low. No inter-rater agreement for LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation; no manual validation

Limited theoretical understanding: Step-aware decay (Eq. 8) motivated empirically without principled justification. Why does early randomness work? Why is mean hidden state divergence optimal? Lack theoretical grounding
Generalization concerns: Only 4 models, all 7B-8B scale. No evaluation on larger models, different architectures, or non-mask-diffusion variants. Limited to single prompt examples
Incomplete failure analysis: Table 1 shows varying defense effectiveness but limited discussion. No adversarial examples or case studies of failure modes. Figure 8 shows successes only

strengths: Timely contribution addressing safety vulnerabilities in emerging dLLM paradigm with clear problem formulation
Novel vulnerability characterization through intra-step/inter-step decomposition and identification of Denoising-path Dependence phenomenon
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 4 models, 6 attack methods, and multiple evaluation approaches with strong empirical results (47.9% → 14.7% ASR)
Practical training-free framework with negligible latency overhead and minimal impact on model utility
Well-structured presentation with thorough reproducibility details, ablation studies, and adaptive attack evaluation
weaknesses: Defense mechanisms lack novelty: stochastic annealing is standard noise injection with linear schedule (no justification), block-level audit builds incrementally on existing hidden state detection with ad-hoc probability suppression (Eq. 10)

Critical practical limitation: prompt decomposition into p_origin ⊕ p_template is never rigorously defined and unlikely generalizes beyond known attack templates; severely limits applicability to novel attack paradigms

Hyperparameter selection unprincipled: λ (safety threshold), γ (remask ratio), and M (extra steps) require manual tuning with high sensitivity (Table 8); no method for setting thresholds for new threat types
White-box access requirement fundamentally restricts real-world deployment to scenarios with full model access; not applicable to API-only systems
Adaptive attacks expose vulnerability: gradient-based and threshold-probing attacks maintain 35-84% success rates (Table 9), suggesting fundamental fragility; insufficient analysis of why
Evaluation concerns: baseline GCG ASR of 0% on AdvBench appears unrealistic; high reliance on LLM-as-a-Judge primary metric despite known limitations; human evaluation limited to 200 samples
Narrow threat model: inference-time only, excludes training-time attacks; artificial experimental setup (Section 3.3 token injection) with unclear transfer to realistic scenarios
Missing analysis: no failure case discussion, limited baseline comparisons (only weak baselines), incomplete justification for technical choices (cosine distance, −∞ logits, linear annealing)
